WalkthroughText: A static variable belongs to the class itself, not to any individual object — there is exactly one copy of it, stored in a special class-level pane in memory, and every object of that class reads and writes that same shared copy. A static method also belongs to the class rather than to an object: it runs without needing an instance, so it can only directly use static variables and its own local variables — it has no access to instance fields and no 'this'. This is different from instance variables, where each object gets its own separate copy living inside that object's own memory. In this walkthrough, watch the class-level pane hold the single shared static variable while each object's stack frame and heap box only track its own instance data.

PracticeItems.Explanation: count is static, so all Counter objects share the exact same class-level variable. Each constructor call increments the shared count once: after c1 it's 1, after c2 it's 2, after c3 it's 3. Since id = count is assigned inside the constructor, c3's id becomes 3. The answer 1 would be wrong because that confuses id (instance-specific, set once) with count continuing to change afterward.

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which of the following is a valid reason to declare a method as static in a class?
Choices: The method needs to access and modify instance variables of a specific object
The method performs a calculation that does not depend on any instance data and should be callable without creating an object
The method must be able to use the keyword 'this' to refer to the calling object
The method overrides a method from a superclass
PracticeItems.Explanation: Static methods belong to the class itself, not to any object, so they are appropriate when no instance data is needed and you want to call the method via the class name alone (e.g., Math.sqrt(x)). The first choice is wrong because static methods cannot directly access instance variables — there's no implicit object. The third choice is wrong because 'this' refers to the calling object, and static methods have no calling object.

totalDeposits is a static (class-level) variable, so it persists across separate calls and is shared — there's only one copy no matter how many times deposit() is called or how many Bank objects (if any) exist. The two calls add 100 and then 50 to the same variable, giving 150. Answer 50 would incorrectly assume each call resets or uses a fresh totalDeposits.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Here's our class: Counter has a static variable count shared by the whole class, and an instance variable id that belongs to each individual object.
We call 'new Counter()' for c1. A stack frame for the constructor is pushed, and a new Counter object is allocated on the heap with its own id field.
Inside the constructor, count++ modifies the ONE shared static variable in the class pane, not anything inside c1's object box.
Then id = count copies the current shared value (1) into c1's own instance field — this copy now lives inside c1's heap box, separate from the class pane.
Now we call 'new Counter()' again for c2. A fresh stack frame and a fresh heap object appear, but notice: there is still only ONE count in the class pane.
count++ runs again — it updates the same shared class-level variable, now becoming 2. Both c1 and c2 'see' this same cell if they ever read it directly.
id = count copies 2 into c2's own id field. c2's id is independent of c1's id — each object keeps its own instance copy, even though they both read from the same static source.
Finally, imagine a static method Counter.getCount() is called directly on the class — no object needed at all. It pushes a stack frame but there's no heap object tied to it.

Summary: the class pane holds one shared static count that every object updates and reads, while each object's own heap box holds its private id — that's the key difference between static and instance data.
